fixes.explanation: Water it is, friend. The text says the water was plentiful at Aenon near Salim, and people kept coming to be baptized. That's the reason John is there. I pick my bakery spot the same way, right next to the oven.

The Sabbath is a big topic in the Gospels, so I see why it came to mind. But it isn't what this argument is about. The text says the dispute was over ceremonial washing. Sometimes an argument just stays on one subject, which is more than I can say for a group chat.
Ha, I see why you'd flip it around. But the disciples say it the other way. They say everyone is going to Jesus, not asking for John. John's next words are about where all of this comes from.

John doesn't go after how Jesus baptizes or who taught Him. His first words are “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.” He points to heaven as the giver, and teachers never come up. I think that's a calm way to answer a report like that.

Afraid is a fair thing to guess when the talk is about crowds going to Jesus. But John's wedding picture isn't scary at all. The friend of the bridegroom is overjoyed to hear his voice, and John says, “That joy is mine, and it is now complete.” It's a happy sound.

I get why sorry came to mind after that report about the crowds. But John says the friend is overjoyed, not sorry. Hearing the bridegroom's voice makes the friend happy. It's a wedding, friend, and nobody there needs to apologize for being glad.

Yes. John says, “He must increase; I must decrease.” That's where his answer to his disciples lands, after he begins with “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.” He's the friend of the bridegroom, and he's glad to see the bridegroom take center stage.

Close, but John gives a different line to the earthly speaker. The one from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. About the One who comes from heaven, John says He is above all. Different source, different description.
Right. John says, “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.” All things, with nothing held back. The statement is simple and complete, so "only some" doesn't fit.
